title: Images and Icons
lead: May Christians make pictures and statues of Christ and the saints, and may they honor them in worship? The law forbids making an idol, yet God also commanded carved cherubim for the tabernacle. Churches have argued over this since the eighth century, and they still differ.

sections.b: "You must not make yourself an idol, or the form of anything up in the sky, or down on the earth, or in the waters below the land" (Exodus 20:4). Moses grounds this in what Israel saw at Sinai: "You saw no form of any kind on the day the LORD spoke to you at Horeb" (Deuteronomy 4:15). The golden calf shows the danger (Exodus 32). Yet God told Moses to make gold cherubim over the ark (Exodus 25:18–22), Solomon's temple was carved with cherubim, palm trees and flowers (1 Kings 6:23–29), and Moses made a bronze snake that healed those who looked at it (Numbers 21:8–9). Later, Hezekiah smashed that same snake because people burned incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). In the New Testament, Christ is "the image of the God who cannot be seen" (Colossians 1:15), and the Word became flesh (John 1:14).
sections.refs: Exodus 20:4–5; Deuteronomy 4:15–19; Exodus 32:1–8; Exodus 25:18–22; 1 Kings 6:23–29; Numbers 21:8–9; 2 Kings 18:4; Colossians 1:15; John 1:14

sections.b: Early Christians painted pictures in the catacombs, and the third-century synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria had painted Bible scenes, so images were not foreign to Jews or Christians. In 726 the Byzantine emperor began a campaign against icons, called iconoclasm ("image-breaking"). John of Damascus answered that because God became visible in Christ, Christ may be pictured. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) ruled that icons may be honored with veneration, while worship belongs to God alone, and that the honor passes to the one the image shows. The dispute ended in the East in 843, a victory the Orthodox still celebrate each year.

Orthodox worship is full of icons, which believers kiss and bow before. Catholics also honor images and statues, following Nicaea II and the Council of Trent. Lutherans kept crucifixes and pictures as teaching aids and opposed those who smashed them, though they do not venerate them. Reformed churches, following Calvin, read the second commandment as forbidding any image of God, and many forbid pictures of Christ; the Heidelberg Catechism says God wants his people taught by the preaching of his word, not by images. Many Baptist, Anabaptist and Quaker churches worship in plain rooms. The way churches number the Ten Commandments reflects this debate: Catholics and Lutherans count the image ban as part of the first commandment, while Orthodox and Reformed count it as a separate second.

common: Christians agree that images must never be worshiped as gods.
uncommon: Some Reformed Christians hold that even teaching pictures of Jesus in children's books break the second commandment.
